headlines.title: Traffic alerts: I-80 Carquinez Bridge closure, limited Highway 101 access in SF
headlines.description: Construction projects on both sides of the Bay this weekend are expected to cause delays for motorists. Here’s what to know about the projects and how to plan ahead. Westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 to shut down Caltrans will close the westbound Carquinez Bridge on Interstate 80 for 53 hours starting Friday night as crews work on a deck rehabilitation project. The closure will start at 10 p.m. and continue through the weekend. It is scheduled to end by 3 a.m. Monday. The eastbound direction of the bridge will remain open. The San Francisco Bay Ferry said it would provide additional ferry trips Saturday and Sunday on the Vallejo route during the westbound closure. The exact closure will be westbound I-80 between the east end of the bridge and start of the westbound off-ramp to Pomona Street, from Sonoma Boulevard, Sequoia Avenue, Magazine Street and Lincoln Road. Below is a map of the closure: Detours during weekend Carquinez Bridge closure Motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento can take the following alternate routes: Detour for westbound I-80 traffic (before Exit 4): Take exit 40 to merge onto southbound Interstate 680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Highway 4 Continue on westbound Highway 4 Take exit 1B, merge onto westbound I-80 To completely avoid the Carquinez Bridge closure, motorists can use westbound I-680. Regional detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Detour for southbound Highway 29 traffic: Detour to Curtola Parkway and stay in the through lane at the Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street intersection to merge onto eastbound Interstate 780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound I-80 Detour for South Vallejo/Carquinez Heights traffic: Detour to northbound Highway 29 (Sonoma Boulevard) Make a right turn onto Lemon Street Continue on Lemon Street and make a right turn at Curtola Parkway/Lemon Street to merge onto eastbound I-780 Continue on eastbound I-780 and stay in the left lane Take exit 7B to merge onto southbound I-680 Continue on southbound I-680 Take exit 53 to merge onto westbound Hwy. 4 Continue on westbound Hwy. 4 Take exit 1B to merge onto westbound I-80 Local detour map for motorists traveling westbound from Sacramento (Caltrans) Limited Highway 101 access in San Francisco Starting Friday at 11 p.m., Caltrans will close two lanes in each direction of the Highway 101 Bayshore Freeway (Hospital Curve) area in San Francisco and expects to keep them closed until 6 a.m. Monday. The impacted portion of Highway 101 will be between Cesar Chavez and 17th streets so Caltrans can work on Hospital Curve rehabilitation, which is part of a longer-term project that started in 2025. Another closure is planned for Sept. 4-7. How to avoid Highway 101 traffic Caltrans is suggesting Interstate 280 or public transportation as an option as they shutter the lanes to work on the median near Hospital Curve. Bay City News contributed to this report. San Francisco 21 hours ago Transportation Jul 20 Caltrans releases Bay Area transit plan to improve access on state highways

headlines.title: Backcountry guide company faces $150K in fines after California's deadliest modern avalanche
headlines.description: California workplace safety officials have fined a guide company that was leading backcountry skiers down a mountain in February when an avalanche was triggered, killing nine members of the group in the deadliest avalanche in the state’s modern history. The California Division of Occupational Safety and Health, or Cal/OSHA, issued $151,300 in fines against Blackbird Mountain Guides for seven alleged violations it found. The largest fine, $81,000, was for “failing to correct the imminent hazard posed by traveling in avalanche terrain when the avalanche danger was rated high.” The agency issued the fines earlier this month. Blackbird Mountain Guides said it has filed a formal appeal and that it believes it was in “full compliance” with all regulatory requirements. A separate investigation by Cal/OSHA’s Bureau of Investigations, which reviews workplace deaths for possible criminal charges, is ongoing, the agency said in a Friday statement. The Nevada County Sheriff’s Department has forwarded results of its own criminal investigation to the district attorney’s office for review of possible criminal charges, said Ashley Quadros, a spokesperson with the sheriff’s office. The DA’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The nine people who died were part of a group of 15 backcountry skiers headed out on a three-day trek organized by Blackbird Mountain Guides into pristine wilderness near Frog Lake in California’s Sierra Nevada as a powerful winter stormmoved into the state. Three of the dead were guides. Northern California Aug 9 Sierra Nevada Apr 6 California Apr 2 The skiers made their way to remote huts located at 7,600 feet (2,316 meters) in Tahoe National Forest, carrying their own food and supplies. Two days later, on Feb. 17, the group was attempting to ski down the mountain when an avalanche hit near Castle Peak, trapping them. Six skiers, including one guide, were rescued after sheltering in place for hours as searchers battled blizzard conditions to reach them. Cal/OSHA, which issued the fines on Aug. 12, found the company allegedly failed “to correct the imminent hazard posed by traveling in avalanche terrain when the avalanche danger was rated high.” The other five violations are related to alleged workplace violations, including not providing employees with effective training and failing to report the three employees’ deaths to the agency in a timely manner. “The citations do not reflect the reality of our profession or the safety program we have built,” Blackbird Mountain Guides said in a statement. “Mountain guiding takes place in dynamic wilderness environments where conditions change minute to minute — it’s not a controlled setting such as construction sites. We welcome the opportunity to work with Cal/OSHA to contextualize the unique realities of operating in backcountry environments.” The guides on the trip had years of experience in backcountry skiing and certifications from the American Mountain Guides Association, which offers the highest level of training in the industry, the company said. “Guides pursue knowledge and excellence as a lifelong responsibility and the guides on this trip approached their work with care and professionalism,” said Blackbird Mountain Guides owner Zeb Blais.
headlines.source: Olga R. Rodriguez | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Active police investigation in Fremont
headlines.description: A police investigation is underway Friday in Fremont. The Fremont Police Department said as of 1:15 p.m. the public should avoid the area of San Pedro Drive between Nicolet Avenue and Frobisher Drive due to police activity. Police said there is no immediate threat to the community while police investigate. No other information was immediately available. headlines.title: 2 injured in Pittsburg house fire
headlines.description: Two people were injured in a Pittsburg house fire Friday morning, with one person taken to a hospital with second- and third-degree burns. Contra Costa County Fire Protection District crews were sent to the home at 69 Atherton Ave. at about 11:40 a.m. and were able to knock down the single-alarm blaze by about 11:45 a.m., according to Fire Capt. Victor Daniel. One person was treated at the scene for smoke inhalation and one person suffered burns that required hospitalization, Daniel said. Fire officials announced at a little after noon that the fire was extinguished, but crews were still at the scene and people are being asked to stay away from the area. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

headlines.title: California officials warn against invasive species
headlines.description: If not managed properly, invasive species in California could further harm local ecology, damage infrastructure and impact economic activity, state officials and experts said during a virtual briefing Thursday. The golden mussel and the glassy-winged sharpshooter were among invasive species discussed in the briefing by representatives from the California Natural Resources Agency, Department of Water Resources, Department of Food and Agriculture, and the Department of Pesticide Regulation. Golden mussels are an invasive freshwater species of mussel, originally from Southeast Asia. The species was first detected in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta in October 2024, and authorities do not know how they arrived in California, said Kristopher Jones, an assistant manager at the California Department of Water Resources. Since then, Jones said, the mussels have spread to water bodies all over the state. “They’re moving pretty quickly since they were detected,” he said. “They’re becoming an infrastructure and water supply issue.” In April, the San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors proclaimed a local emergency because of golden mussels and their impacts on the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. Jones explained that the mussels proliferate fast, competing with native species of aquatic life, and attach to hard surfaces like the bottom of boats, pipes and other water infrastructure. As a result, they can clog waterways and damage vital water infrastructure. Jones said that the Department of Water Resources and the Department of Fish and Wildlife are working to use different treatment methods. To avoid inadvertently spreading the golden mussels, Jones urged watercraft users, “before you move your boat from one water body to another, clean it, drain it completely and let it dry.” Another invasive pest is threatening California’s winegrape industry — the glassy-winged sharpshooter. The glassy-winged sharpshooter is a leafhopper insect and spreads the fatal grapevine ailment known as Pierce’s disease, a bacterial infection that blocks water-conducting systems in plants, causing them to dry out. The disease is incurable. In May, the California Department of Food and Agriculture found that grapevines infested with the insect were supplied to multiple Costco locations across California. The plants, numbering in the thousands, came from Burchell Nursery in Fresno County. Since then, the California Department of Food and Agriculture and county agricultural officials have been tracking the pest, setting up traps, and destroying infested grapevines to prevent further spread. A 2025 study funded in part by the Pierce’s Disease/Glassy-Winged Sharpshooter Board at the California Department of Food and Agriculture estimated that if the pest is allowed to spread unchecked, it could cost the state’s winegrape growers an additional $56 million a year in lost production and vine replacement. The pest already costs growers roughly $48 million in lost winegrape production and vine replacement every year, the study added. Attacking the pest early on is the best shot at controlling its spread, as small and isolated populations are easier to tackle, said Jeff Dukes, senior staff scientist at the Carnegie Institution for Science. A winegrape industry group has committed $820,000 to the effort, and the CDFA estimates that it spent $3.2 million in its initial response in May and June. “When you spend money on catching new invaders early, that can make a big difference because you can get rid of the invading population,” Dukes said.

headlines.title: Protesters who shut down the Golden Gate Bridge face sentencing
headlines.description: Seven protesters who were convicted of blocking the Golden Gate Bridge at the start of the Israel-Hamas war will be sentenced by a San Francisco judge Friday. Six protesters are facing a maximum sentence of five years, while the seventh faces up to five and a half years. Sentencing is scheduled to take place at 1:30 p.m. Back in 2024, protesters shut down the Golden Gate Bridge for hours during the morning commute. The protesters, dubbed the “Golden Gate 26,” were eventually arrested and hit with multiple charges, including false imprisonment. The majority of the protesters avoided trial, but seven of them went through a weekslong trial that ended with a guilty verdict for false imprisonment. The protesters narrowly avoided a more severe charge of felony conspiracy, which could have carried a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison. San Francisco Jul 2 San Francisco May 20 Protesters face trial over Golden Gate Bridge shutdown

headlines.title: Bee the change: Californians asked to choose a State Bee
headlines.description: California has a lot of official “things”. The California redwood is the official tree, the poppy is the official flower, and the Garibaldi is the official marine state fish. And yet, we’ve never had an official bee, even though the Golden State has more bees than almost any other state. That’s where YOU come in. Out of 1,600 bee species that call California home, the California Native Bee Society picked 19 types and they’re asking the public to vote on the bee that they think best represents the state. The initiative is part of a statewide effort to find California’s official bee. You can browse the selection of bees and vote on the California Native Bee Society’s website here. If you’re planning to vote, be a busy bee about it, because voting closes Sept. 8! And if you’re curious about other official state symbols, click here. headlines.title: Front yard chessboard brings 12-year-old Ukrainian immigrant peace, community
headlines.description: Like many talented young chess players, 12-year-old Max Tsebrii started playing at an early age. “I started playing chess at five,” Max said. In other words, chess has been a constant throughout most of his life. One of the few constants, as it turns out. When Max first learned the game, his family was living in Odesa, Ukraine. He was 8 years old when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. “I remember we were hiding in the hallways of the house when the alarms went off,” Max recalled. “It was pretty scary.” His mother, Lina, knew they could not stay. “We were living through the war for one year, and he was under a lot of stress,” she said. “He was crying. He was trembling because of the bombs.” After spending time in Germany, the family eventually settled in Alameda. For Max, playing chess online provided a sense of familiarity and comfort in a new country. But it could also be lonely. So last summer, he came up with an idea. Max carried a table, two chairs, and a chessboard into his front yard and invited anyone passing by to play a game. Win or lose, each opponent would receive a homemade cookie. Lina spread the word in a local Alameda Facebook group, letting neighbors know that Max was ready and waiting for challengers. The response exceeded their expectations. “It means a lot,” Max said. “I’ve met a lot of people. Last summer, I played about 150 games.” Lina said the community quickly embraced her son. “When I make Facebook posts about his chess stand, people are so supportive,” she said. “He’s played with police officers, postal workers, and lots of kids. Sometimes there’s a crowd around his chess table, and he’s very happy.” Max’s front yard chess stand has become much more than a place to play the game he loves. For a young refugee adjusting to life in a new country, it has helped transform loneliness into friendship and community. And for Max, the experience has brought a little local fame as well. How does it make him feel? “Famous,” he said with a laugh.

headlines.title: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab wins special election to succeed Eric Swalwell in Congress
headlines.description: What to Know State Sen. Aisha Wahab has won a special election for California’s Congressional District 14, NBC News projects. The Congressional District 14 seat was vacated earlier this year when former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell resigned from Congress after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. Wahab will fill Swalwell’s seat through January. At that time, the winner of the regular general election in November will take over for a full, two-year term. California’s 14th Congressional District includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. California lawmaker Aisha Wahab secured victory Thursday in a special election to serve the rest of former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s House term, which ends in January. Swalwell, a Democrat who was running for California governor, ended his campaign and resigned from Congress in April after he was accused of sexual assault and harassment. He has denied the allegations. Wahab defeated Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez in the special election in the state’s 14th Congressional District, which covers parts of Alameda County on the eastern side of the San Francisco Bay. Wahab has championed housing affordability and access. She also wrote a bill in 2023 to ban caste-based discrimination, which garnered national attention. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed it, saying such discrimination is already outlawed by civil rights protections. Wahab became the first Afghan American elected to public office in the U.S. when she won a Hayward City Council seat in 2018. She’ll be the first Afghan American to serve in Congress. The conclusion of the race to replace Swalwell comes as criminal investigations continue into the sexual assault allegations he faces. Over the weekend, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and later searched his home in Washington D.C., according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity. California Aug 20 Decision 2026 Aug 18 Swalwell’s attorney did not immediately respond to an email and phone message seeking comment. Wahab and Hernandez will face off again in a separate November election determining who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab won the June primary decisively, but she’s been up against a swell of spending boosting her rival ahead of the general. Groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, poured millions into supporting Hernandez, and thousands into opposing Wahab. Hernandez issued the following statement Thursday after the race was called: “I’ve been a fighter my whole life, and when I promised the residents of CA-14 I would fight for them, I never gave up. In just 63 days, we closed a gap from 26,000 votes to 6,000 votes by sharing our message of lowering housing costs, creating jobs, and supporting strong public safety. Voters finally got the chance to see what I have been doing as a mom, Dublin’s Mayor, and a director of healthcare services. The election for CA-14 in November will be in the new district lines, adding 26,000 Dublin voters who didn’t have the chance to vote for me in August. We’re looking forward to winning this on November 3rd with a more favorable district and a much larger electorate. Game on!” Associated Press reporter Alanna Drukin Richer contributed from Washington.

headlines.title: Proposed indoor shooting range in Walnut Creek sparks debate
headlines.description: A proposal to transform a vacant commercial building into a nine-lane shooting range in Walnut Creek has drawn mixed reaction for people living nearby. The proposal from Elite Armory would transform a former carpet store on North Main Street into a nine-lane indoor shooting range with firearms training, instructional classes and retail sales. The company also wants to expand the existing building, add parking and make other exterior improvements. The building is located in a commercial area surrounded by businesses like car dealerships and auto service shops. Serge has lived in Walnut Creek for years and as someone who goes to shooting ranges, he says he’d welcome one closer to home. “Honestly speaking, I’m fine with it. We don’t have many shooting ranges here,” he said. But opposition also emerged during Wednesday’s Design Review Commission meeting, with some questioning whether a shooting range belongs in this part of the city. Those who spoke at the meeting say the area is also close to homes and families, and question whether a gun range fits the character of the neighborhood. Elite Armory’s Co-Owner Gabriel Casillas says safety is at the center of the design. “Thank you for the option to speak today and give some more background on our business,” Casillas said. The proposed range would have a ballistic ceiling,impact-resistant walls and sound-absorbing materials. The company also presented a noise study saying the range would not have a significant impact on the surrounding area. The debate isn’t one-sided; the city says it received 101 emails about the proposal with 54% opposed and 44% in support. The city says it wants residents to stay involved as the project moves through the review process. “We encourage residents and other interested parties to continue participating in the public review process as the application moves through the public review process,” the city said in a statement. For some residents, support or opposition may ultimately come down to how the range would operate. “If it’s done right, it’s fine. Just like anything else, there has to be risk management, and you have to be aware of the surroundings you know,” Walnut Creek resident Orbie Diaz Said. The Design Review Commission will make a recommendation on the project, but it will not make the final decision. The next major step will be a hearing before the Walnut Creek Planning Commission where the conditional use permit will be considered. That meeting has not yet been scheduled. Any decision there could later be appealed to the City Council.

headlines.title: Coastal farmworkers feel the squeeze: ‘The money coming in just isn't enough'
headlines.description: Working full-time picking strawberries and watering trees for minimum wage wasn’t enough to put food on his family’s table, so Pescadero farmworker Margarito Gomez said he decided to grow his own. “The word minimum says it all,” said Gomez, a husband and father of four who moved to the area 25 years ago. “It’s the minimum to survive.” When Gomez wraps up his day job every afternoon, he heads over to Gavilanes Farm, the farm he owns and operates with friends on land they lease from a neighbor. The farm – which mostly grows beans and tomatoes – helps guarantee his family will have healthy food to eat. “We’re taking it very seriously,” he said. “Right now we’re farming four acres.” But so far, the farm isn’t making a profit and Gomez said he also does maintenance work for his landlord in exchange for a discount on the rent. He’s not the only one feeling the squeeze. The coastal towns that house many of the county’s farmworkers may feel worlds away from Silicon Valley, but the cost of living is still in line with the Bay Area. The annual per-capita income in San Mateo County is roughly $84,000, according to recent U.S. Census data, but the number dips to roughly $59,000 in Pescadero and significantly less than that for the region’s minimum wage workers. Housing costs alone quickly eat up earnings. Three-bedroom homes like the one rented by Gomez and his family are listed for $4,000 or more on sites such as Zillow. Then there’s everything else. “Right now, the money coming in just isn’t enough.” said Irma Flores, who should be retired but works caring for an elderly adult to help make ends meet. “Everything is so expensive.” Like many in the community, Flores relies on outside help to get by. She was among dozens of people – mostly mothers – lined up outside a Pescadero school to load up on groceries provided for free by ALAS, a local nonprofit that serves coastal farmworkers in Northern California. “We’re just really grateful to be able to provide culturally appropriate foods that we know our families are going to use in their kitchens,” said ALAS Farmworker and Essential Worker Program Director Sandra Sencion. Volunteers pack food into bags alongside the organization’s Farmworker Equity Express Bus, which travels the area providing free resources, from food and basic necessities to educational and mental health services. Some of the produce was purchased directly from Gavilanes Farm, the farm operated by Margarito Gomez. “It’s a very special bus,” Sencion said. “Really connecting with our community to be able to bring them the services that are really challenging to get for some of our farmworkers and essential workers.” For people like Flores, the program helps relieve some of that economic stress. “This helps us because every week they bring something different,” she said. “One week it’s food. Another week, it’s clothing, soap or other essentials.” Leydi Cervantes was also in line. She arrived in Pescadero nearly 32 years ago as a teenager and is now married with four children. “Both parents have to work and sometimes that’s still not enough,” said Cervantes, who earns a living packing lettuce. “So, one of them has to take a second job. My husband finishes work here, then goes to another job at a horse ranch.” Sometimes it’s still not enough. “When we just can’t make it, we apply for financial assistance programs that help us pay the rent,” she said. Like many farmworkers here, Cervantes rents her home and said she has given up hope of owning her own. According to Zillow, the average home price in Pescadero currently hovers north of $1 million. San Mateo County officials have identified a shortage of affordable housing in Pescadero and in neighboring Half Moon Bay, which now faces a lawsuit from the state for failing to comply with mandated housing plans. One of the proposed developments at the center of this battle is the 555 Kelly Avenue project, a landmark 40-unit affordable housing complex for elderly farmworkers. It was originally proposed in 2022 and propelled forward after the 2023 mass shooting in Half Moon Bay that exposed the substandard living conditions of local farmworkers. Despite the lack of affordable housing in the area, there’s been local opposition to the project from some residents and city leaders regarding density and traffic concerns. Following a successful local petition drive, the project’s fate now rests in the hands of voters on the upcoming November ballot. In the meantime, Cervantes and other farmworkers say they’ll keep pushing forward, leaning on the community for help when necessary. “Keep going,” Cervantes said. “Anything is possible. And don’t be ashamed to ask for help.”
headlines.source: Hilda Gutierrez, Michael Bott, Son Vo, Robbie Beasom and Jeremy Carroll

headlines.title: Many upset after community murals on East San Jose building painted over
headlines.description: Many were upset after two murals outside of a building sold about a year ago in East San Jose were painted over by the building’s new owner. A social media post by nonprofit ConXión says Martha’s Kitchen painted over two community murals on the outside of the building ConXión sold to them in 2025. “No warning, nothing else was painted, so it wasn’t like they were painting the whole building, it was just those things,” President and CEO of ConXión Lori Chávez said. “The murals themselves have a lot of significance because it shows history.” Chávez says one of the murals was created with young people who participated in an after-school program for native American and Latino students. “That mural was done by Jimmy Fonseca and it was done in collaboration with the youth, with kids at the after-school program,” Chávez said. Chávez says ConXión discussed the murals with Martha’s Kitchen during negotiations to sell the building. “We told them, we love these murals, they’re important to the community, we’d like for you to keep them, inside and out, and he agreed, ‘Yes they’re beautiful, we’ll keep them’,” Chávez said. But Martha’s Kitchen Executive Director Bill Lee says that conversation never happened. “They never raised the issue, and that’s one of the reasons I’m very disappointed with that social media post because they never asked us to preserve the mural,” Lee said. Lee says Martha’s Kitchen told ConXión in October that it intended to paint over the murals. He says the exterior needed to be painted, and the murals did not represent Martha’s Kitchen’s mission. “Unfortunately, the mural neither represents what our organization does, we feed people who are starving, we feed the homeless,” Lee said. Lee says Martha’s Kitchen plans to put a new mural on a nearby wall, one that he says will reflect the organization’s work. “That mural will represent food being grown, food being prepared, food being consumed which is what we do, we’re here for the community, we rescue food that would otherwise go into the landfill and feed people that would otherwise go hungry,” Lee said. ConXión says the murals represented an important part of the community’s story. Martha’s Kitchen says it plans to replace them with artwork that better reflects its mission. San Jose City Councilman Bien Doan sent a statement addressing the situation. “I was very disappointed to see the murals were covered up. I know Martha’s Kitchen wants to be a good neighbor, but that means respecting and embracing our cultural values and histories, especially with respect to our children. It is my hope that this mural will be replaced soon and that they incorporate imaging representative of our youth and indigenous residents,” he wrote.
